message.content: can you explain to me how this board thing even works im confused

content.text:
The board is a shared chat for the team, and it lives in one pinned GitHub issue (issue #1 in the `e-yang6/uncle` repo). Each post is a comment on that issue. You, Ethan, Isaac and all your Claude agents read and write there, so everyone sees what changed and who needs to do what.

**Why it exists:** each person has their own Claude agent working in separate folders. The agents can't see each other's sessions, so the board is how they coordinate. For example, if I need Isaac's head files in a certain format, I post on the board and tag him.

**How you use it, through `tools/board`:**
- `tools/board unread` shows new posts since you last checked, and flags any that mention you.
- `tools/board read -n 20` shows the last 20 posts.
- `tools/board post "[Jeffrey's Claude] text"` writes a post. The prefix says whose agent wrote it.
- `tools/board whoami` shows which GitHub account the tool is using.
- `tools/board wait` blocks until someone else posts. The rules say not to leave it running, because every wake-up costs credits.

**Tagging:** use GitHub usernames. @e-yang6 is Ethan, @jeffreywongg is you, @personalisaacw is Isaac, and @all is everyone. If a post tags you, you do the work and reply. If it doesn't, you only read it, and you only change course if it affects your folders.

**Automatic checks:** a hook in `.claude/settings.json` shows unread posts when a session starts and on every prompt. That's why Ethan's hello appeared at the start of this session.

**What I did:** I replied to Ethan's hello using `tools/board post`. That is a normal comment on the GitHub issue, so you can also read it in the browser at the link I gave you.

message.content: yes but how do know when i get pinged though and wil lyou be able to take those flagged issues?

content.text:
There are two separate answers, one for you and one for me.

**How you get pinged**
- **GitHub itself:** a post that tags `@jeffreywongg` is a normal GitHub mention. You get a GitHub notification, and an email if your notification settings allow it. That works even when no Claude session is open.
- **Inside Claude Code:** the hook in `.claude/settings.json` runs `tools/board unread` when a session starts and on every prompt you send. Any post that mentions you is flagged `MENTION` and shows up in my context. That's how I saw Ethan's hello.

**Whether I'll take those flagged posts**
- I only see the board when a session is running and a hook fires. That's at session start and each time you send a prompt. If you're idle and I'm not running, I see nothing.
- When I see a `MENTION`, the rules say I act on it and reply on the board. If the request touches voice/ or server/, I'll do it. If it touches someone else's folders, I'll flag that to you instead of editing them.
- Anything bigger than a small fix, I'll propose as a plan first and wait for your OK, as CLAUDE.md requires.

**The gap:** there's no live push from the board into my session. The hook output suggests running `tools/board wait` in the background. It wakes me when a new post arrives, but AGENTS.md says not to leave it running because it burns credits. Without it, I only catch mentions when you send a prompt.

Practical setup: leave GitHub notifications on so you hear about mentions, and I'll catch them each time you prompt me. If you're expecting something urgent from a teammate, tell me and I'll start a single `tools/board wait` for that stretch. Do you want that?

content.text:
Yes, that works, and it's the simplest way to run it.

1. Ethan posts on the board, then tells you in person or in chat.
2. You tell me something like "check the board." I run `tools/board unread` and read what he wrote.
3. If it touches voice/ or server/, I'll propose a short plan and wait for your OK, since that's the rule in CLAUDE.md. For a small fix I'll just do it.
4. When it's done, I post a reply on the board tagging Ethan, so he knows without you relaying it.

You may not even need to tell me. The hook shows unread posts every time you send a prompt, so any new post, especially one that mentions you, will already be in front of me on your next message.

If Ethan asks for something in someone else's folder, like Isaac's head/ or xr/, I won't edit it. I'll tell you and post on the board so it reaches the right person.

I couldn't read the PDF, and I haven't changed anything. The reader needs `poppler` (`pdftoppm`), which isn't installed, and no other PDF tool on your Mac works either. There are two ways to fix that:

- **Install poppler:** run `! brew install poppler` in the prompt. Then I can read the PDF directly.
- **Skip the PDF:** `PLAN.md` in the repo looks like the same plan, and I've already read it. If the PDF has something that isn't in `PLAN.md`, paste that part here.

## My plan, assuming the PDF matches PLAN.md

The board has no new posts, and BUILD.md's kickoff time is still blank. So I'm treating us as in hours 0–4, the thin version. My folders are `voice/` and `server/`. This is what's on my list in BUILD.md, in order:

**Step 1: Server skeleton in `server/` (about 30 min)**
- `npm start` on port 3000 serves a static page, and a health endpoint says which features are off (no ElevenLabs key, no Gemini key).
- It starts fine with no keys, as the rules require.
- Done when: `curl localhost:3000/health` shows each feature's status.

**Step 2: One-line voice loop in `voice/` (the hours 0–4 task)**
- Send one hardcoded sentence to ElevenLabs text-to-speech and get audio back.
- Write the first version of the aging filter (pitch, wobble, breathiness, pace, tone) and apply it to that audio.
- Stream the result from the server to a browser page.
- Done when: a button on the page plays the aged line, and I give you a measured delay.
- Fallback with no ElevenLabs key: a stock sample voice, then text.

**Step 3: Agree the voice endpoint with Ethan**
- CONTRACTS.md has "Voice pipeline: fill in at kickoff", so I'd post a proposed socket or endpoint on the board for Ethan to approve, and Isaac needs it too, so his mouth animation can read the audio.
- I won't build against it until it's agreed.

**Then, in order:** interview, Gemini extraction and the confirm screen (hours 4–12), streaming under 1.5 s (hours 12–20), and fallbacks (hours 20–26).

**Questions for you:**
1. Do you want to install poppler, or should I go from PLAN.md?
2. Do you have an ElevenLabs key yet? It's on the "Humans only" list. Without it I'd build the server and the filter against a placeholder.
3. Is this plan OK to start with Step 1?

content.content:
Uncle: Project Plan




  Uncle: Project Plan
     Nov 10, 2026 · ​@ethan



  The idea
  Uncle puts you in a headset and sits you across from yourself at 70: a 3D version of your
  own head, aged, talking in an aged version of your own voice. Everything it tells you about
  your life comes from a Monte Carlo simulation we built, fed by official Canadian data, and
  spoken by a model we fine-tuned so it can't invent numbers. Change one thing, like "save
  $50 more a month," and you watch your future self change in front of you, using controls
  right there in the headset.

  One-liner: "Meet the future you, who can't make things up."

  Why it matters. People treat their future selves like strangers, so they under-save and
  under-invest in their health. In Hal Hershfield's research, people who saw an aged image
  of themselves put nearly twice as much into a retirement fund as people who saw their
  current face.

  What already exists, and what's new. The "talk to your future self" idea has been done, so
  the novelty has to come from the engineering:


     Prior version                 What it does                     What it lacks

     MIT Media Lab Future You      Text chat with an aged           No voice; a reviewer found
     (2024 research)               photo, built from a life-story   its answers mostly generic
                                   questionnaire

     Mirror8 (Gemini Live Agent    Selfie to 8 possible futures,    Not your voice, no real
     Challenge 2026)               then a live voice                numbers behind it
                                   conversation

     TalkTuahFutureYou (Nosu AI    Chat with your future self       Text only, no grounding, no
     Hackathon winner)             about money, with timelines      face or voice


  Uncle adds things none of them have: a full 3D head of you built from a short video, aged
  visually and talking in mixed reality; your own voice, aged by our own audio code; a
  simulation engine using real, live Canadian data; a fine-tuned model that can only point to
  the simulation's numbers, never invent its own; and sliders in the headset that reshape
  your future self, money and health, as you adjust your choices.



                                                                                              Page 1 of 20
 Uncle: Project Plan




  The experience
  A full session takes about 4 to 5 minutes, and the judge is the subject.

      1. Head scan (30 seconds). A teammate films a 24-second video while you slowly turn
         around, keeping a neutral face. Your 3D head starts building in the background
          straight away (Part 3). For judging, heads can also be scanned on a judge's first visit to
          the table and saved, so they're ready when the judge comes back; a saved teammate
          head is the fallback.
      2. Quick interview (about 1 minute). In a quiet corner, we ask a few friendly questions
         out loud: your age, roughly what you earn and save, and your habits, like exercise,
         sleep, smoking and drinking. This does two jobs at once: it's the voice sample for the
          clone (Part 4), and Gemini pulls your answers into the simulation's inputs (Part 1).
      3. "Did we get this right?" (5 seconds). A short screen shows what we heard, like "age
          21, saving $100 a month, exercise twice a week," so you can fix anything misheard
          before it shapes every number.
      4. Put on the headset. Through passthrough you still see the real room, and across the
         table, in a mirror frame, is you at 70: your own face, aged, with grey hair. It greets you
         by name in an older version of your own voice.
      5. Talk to them. Ask anything out loud: "Did we ever buy a house?" "Was I okay with
         money?" "How's my health?" Every number in the answer comes from the simulation.
      6. Change your future yourself. Sliders for saving, exercise, sleep and smoking float
         beside the mirror. Pinch and drag them with your own hands (the Quest's hand
         tracking; controllers work too), and your future self changes as you move them: the
         face, the health and money numbers, and what they say. The headset view is cast to a
         laptop screen so everyone around can watch.
      7. Take it off and leave with one concrete next step. A one-page summary: the one
         change that mattered most for your money and your health, its numbers, a link, and
         how to start it today (for example, the exact steps to set up an automatic $50 monthly
         transfer into a TFSA at your bank). If the vault (Part 6) is built, this is where the
         deposit happens. This is the "meaningful action" for Canada Life.

  The "wow" beat is step 4: seeing your own face, older, look at you and say your name in
  your own aged voice. The "oh, this is real" beat is step 6: you drag a slider yourself, and
  the person across the table changes, backed by numbers you can trace.




                                                                                                 Page 2 of 20
 Uncle: Project Plan




  Architecture
  The parts we build are the brain; outside services only listen, clone the voice and
  transcribe. Three pipelines run side by side: the facts sheet ties the numbers to what the
  voice is allowed to say, and the face pipeline turns a 24-second video into the aged head in
  the headset.




  architecture · 3 pipelines, 9 parts built by us

  The highlighted boxes are ours and carry the technical depth: the simulation engine, the
  facts sheet and ranking, the fine-tuned model and its fill-and-check step, the voice aging
  filter, and the whole face pipeline from 3D head build to aging to the talking mouth. The
  simulation also sets each future's apparent age for the face.




                                                                                        Page 3 of 20
 Uncle: Project Plan




  Part 1: the life simulation engine
  The engine is the real product: a Monte Carlo simulation that runs about 5,000 possible
  lives from today to age 100 and reports ranges, not a single guess. It runs fast enough to
  redraw the future every time a slider moves. Its inputs come from the interview, and its
  current rates and limits come from official sources read when the app starts. Owner:
  Person 1.


  Inputs

     Input                        Default if skipped       Used for

     Age, sex                     20, sex-averaged         Starting point, life table

     Province                     Ontario                  Taxes and benefits (simplified)

     Income per year              Median for age           Savings, CPP estimate
                                  group

     Savings now (RRSP, TFSA,     $0                       Starting balancet
     other)

     Saving per month             $0                       Contributions

     Investment mix               60% stocks, 40%          Return draws
                                  bonds

     Retirement age               65                       When contributions stop and
                                                           withdrawals start

     Smoking, exercise, sleep,    Population average       Health and longevity adjustments
     alcohol


  Getting the inputs from the interview. The interview's transcript goes to Gemini, using
  its structured output so it returns clean fields, with one job: fill in the table above as
  structured fields, leaving anything not mentioned on its default. Show the result on the
  "did we get this right?" screen before running anything. Test it on 20 recorded practice
  interviews and report how many fields came out right.


  How one simulated life runs
      1. Step through each year from today's age to 100.




                                                                                              Page 4 of 20
 Uncle: Project Plan




      2. Money: draw that year's stock and bond returns and inflation by resampling real
         historical years, so good and bad years come in realistic runs. Add salary growth and
          contributions, respecting TFSA and RRSP limits.
      3. Retirement: at the retirement age, stop contributing, add estimated CPP and OAS
         income using the government's published formulas and current-year amounts, and
          withdraw what's needed to keep spending steady.
      4. Health: each year, the chance of dying comes from Statistics Canada's life table for
         that age and sex, multiplied by the extra risk from each habit, using published
          research figures. When the simulated person dies, the life ends there.
      5. Record the whole path: balances, income and age at death.


  Outputs
          Ranges for savings at 70, yearly retirement income, the chance the money lasts to 90,
          and life expectancy: shown as "most likely" plus a bad-luck and good-luck case (the
          10th, 50th and 90th percentiles).
          The one change that matters most: rerun with each input nudged a little and rank
          which single change moves the outcomes most. The future self brings this change up,
          and the sliders highlight it.
          A facts sheet: a small structured list of every number the future self is allowed to say,
          which Part 2 checks against.


  Data to collect (all public)

     Data                                        Source

     Death rates by age and sex                  Statistics Canada life tables

     CPP and OAS rules and current               Canada.ca
     amounts

     TFSA and RRSP contribution limits           Canada Revenue Agency

     Inflation history                           Statistics Canada consumer price index

     Historical stock and bond returns           A public dataset of annual index returns (pick one
                                                 and cite it)

     How habits change death risk                Published meta-analyses, one per habit, cited on
                                                 screen




                                                                                               Page 5 of 20
 Uncle: Project Plan




  Current values at startup. When the app starts, a small script reads this year's CPP and
  OAS amounts and TFSA/RRSP limits from Canada.ca. Each value is saved with its source
  link and the time it was read, and that's what the "where this comes from" panel shows.
  Never fetch during a conversation, since it's too slow and too fragile; keep the last good
  copy as a backup in case a page changes.


  How we prove it works
          Against the government's calculator: set the engine to fixed returns and compare it
          with the federal government's Canadian Retirement Income Calculator on 10 to 20
          test profiles. Target: within 5% on each.
          Against Statistics Canada: with all habits at average, the engine's life expectancy
          should match the published figure for that age and sex.
          Unit tests for the CPP, OAS and contribution-limit rules, since a wrong rule shows up
          in every run.
          Speed: 5,000 lives recalculated in under 100 ms, measured on the demo laptop.

  Kept simple on purpose: taxes are approximate, and there's no housing, kids or job
  changes. Say so on screen.


  Part 2: the future self's words
  A small model we fine-tune writes everything the future self says, but it never writes a
  number. It writes placeholders that point into the simulation's facts sheet, and our code
  fills in the real values, so an invented number is impossible rather than caught. Owner:
  Person 1.

  How a reply is made:

      1. The model gets the facts sheet from Part 1, the user's answers, and the question, and
          replies as the user at 70.
      2. It writes placeholders instead of numbers, like: "By 70 I had about
          {savings_70.median} put away, and honestly, {one_change} is what made the
          difference."
      3. Our code checks every placeholder exists in the facts sheet, then fills in the real
          value, rounded the way people speak ("about four hundred thousand").
      4. Advice comes from the simulation, not the model. The "one change that matters
          most" is the simulation's own ranking (Part 1); the model only says it in the future self's
          voice. It never invents new recommendations.



                                                                                               Page 6 of 20
 Uncle: Project Plan




      5. Anything else is blocked. If a reply contains a raw number or an unknown placeholder,
         it's rewritten once; if it fails again, a safe template sentence built straight from the
          facts sheet is used. The voice pipeline only ever receives checked text.

  The future self can make up feelings and colour that don't claim a fact ("I still go walking
  every morning"). Anything about money, health or age has to come from a placeholder.

  The fine-tune:

          Base model: a small open-weight model with a permissive license (a Qwen or Llama
          model of about 3 to 8 billion parameters), fine-tuned with LoRA using a tool like
          Unsloth on a Vultr cloud GPU, using the free credits from MLH's Vultr track. Tessera
          did the same kind of fine-tune on an A100 in about 44 minutes for roughly $24.
          Training data: about 1,000 to 3,000 example conversations, generated automatically.
          Each is a random profile run through the simulation, its facts sheet, a question, and a
          reply written with placeholders. Throw out any example with a placeholder that
          doesn't exist. Generate the replies with an open-weight model whose license allows
          training on its outputs, since some major AI providers' terms forbid using their
          outputs to train other models.
          Serving: vLLM on the same Vultr GPU, or llama.cpp on the Mac, streaming sentence
          by sentence into the voice pipeline.
          Timing: practise the training script before the event, then generate the data and train
          at the event. Start generating from about hour 6, train overnight.
          Fallback: Gemini, prompted to use the same placeholder format. If the fine-tune
          sounds flat, swap it in and nothing else changes.

  How we prove it: run the base model, the fine-tuned model and Gemini on the same 200
  test conversations with random profiles and questions.


     Measure                                                Target

     Replies with zero invented numbers                     100% for ours

     Sounds like an older you, not a chatbot (blind-rated   Ours rated at least as high as Gemini
     by people)

     Time to first word                                     Faster than Gemini

     Replies that needed a rewrite                          Under 10%


  That table goes straight onto the prize pages and the demo slide.



                                                                                              Page 7 of 20
 Uncle: Project Plan




  Part 3: your future head in AR
  A full 3D head of the user is built for free on our own Mac from a 24-second video, aged in
  skin, hair and shape according to the simulation, and shown talking from a mirror frame
  across the table in a headset. Owner: Person 3.


  Building the head
  We follow the approach of Punching Face (Hack the North 2026), which documents a fully
  local pipeline. Its repo has no license, so we write our own code from the approach rather
  than copying theirs.

      1. Film it. A teammate films a 24-second video while the person slowly turns their head
         and shoulders through a full turn with a neutral face, using a phone or laptop webcam.
      2. Pick frames and cut out the head. Keep up to about 200 frames, and remove the
         background with MediaPipe's selfie segmentation model. You need at least 24
         overlapping views, 12 of them showing the face.
      3. Recover where the camera was for each frame with COLMAP.
      4. Triangulate the face. Find MediaPipe's 468 face landmarks in the frames and turn
         them into 3D points using those camera positions.
      5. Fit a full head. Warp an open-source head template (MakeHuman: skull, ears and neck
         included) smoothly onto the 3D landmarks, and fit a simple smooth hair shape to the
         head's outline in the frames. A landmark-only face looks like a floating mask; the full
         template fixes that. Check MakeHuman's asset license.
      6. Paint it. Project the frames onto the head, mainly from one frontal frame for the face,
         blending into the side views.

  Skip what costs money or failed for them: their optional hair and back-of-head step used a
  paid AI API, so instead require a full turn so the back of the head is actually filmed. And
  skip Gaussian splats, which came out 31 to 33 mm off the face in their tests.

  Speed and saved heads. Their measured run took about 3 minutes for a 24-second video
  on an M5 Pro Mac, over a minute of it in the paid step we skip. So start the build the
  moment filming ends, and run the interview while it builds. For judging, scan each judge
  on their first visit and save the finished head, so it's ready when they come back. A saved
  teammate head is the fallback if a build fails.




                                                                                            Page 8 of 20
 Uncle: Project Plan




  Aging it
  Aging has to change the skin, the hair and the shape together. Getting only one of them
  right is what looks creepy.

          Skin. Run an open-source face-aging model (one candidate is the published SAM age-
          transformation model; check its license) on every frame used for painting, not just the
          front, on the same Vultr GPU as the fine-tune. Aging only the front leaves young skin
          at the cheeks and temples, with a visible seam. If side views age inconsistently, use
          the aged front for the whole face and fill the sides with matched aged skin tone.
          Hair. The hair shape keeps its original colour unless you change it, so tint it in the 3D
          app toward grey and lighten it, by an amount set by the future's age.
          Shape. Real aging changes shape too: a softer jaw, slight sagging, thinner lips.
          MakeHuman's character settings include an age slider, so after fitting, add the
          difference between the template at the person's age and at 70. Check that the
          exported template carries those age changes, and keep the effect modest.
          Tied to the simulation. Each future gets an "apparent age": its real age, nudged older
          or younger by its health path (for example, a smoking future looks a few years older).
          Keep the nudge small and based on a cited source.

  Making the sliders instant. Prepare a few aged skin versions in advance at different
  apparent ages (about 10 in total). When the person drags a slider in the headset, the
  simulation reruns in under 100 ms, the future's apparent age moves, and the headset
  blends between the two closest skin versions while shifting the shape and hair amounts
  smoothly. All of that runs on the graphics card, so the head changes live as the hand
  moves.

  Building the head
  We follow the approach of Punching Face (Hack the North 2026), which documents a fully
  local pipeline. Its repo has no license, so we write our own code from the approach rather
  than copying theirs.

      1. Film it. A teammate films a 24-second video while the person slowly turns their head
         and shoulders through a full turn with a neutral face, using a phone or laptop webcam.
      2. Pick frames and cut out the head. Keep up to about 200 frames, and remove the
         background with MediaPipe's selfie segmentation model. You need at least 24
         overlapping views, 12 of them showing the face.
      3. Recover where the camera was for each frame with COLMAP.
      4. Triangulate the face. Find MediaPipe's 468 face landmarks in the frames and turn
         them into 3D points using those camera positions.
      5. Fit a full head. Warp an open-source head template (MakeHuman: skull, ears and neck
         included) smoothly onto the 3D landmarks, and fit a simple smooth hair shape to the
         head's outline in the frames. A landmark-only face looks like a floating mask; the full
         template fixes that. Check MakeHuman's asset license.
      6. Paint it. Project the frames onto the head, mainly from one frontal frame for the face,
         blending into the side views.

  applies each change by an amount set by the future's age and health path:

          Wobble: tiny random variations in pitch and loudness, like an older voice's natural

A human decision is anything an agent can't settle itself, so a person has to say yes, no or which one.

○ not set up (run `entire enable` to get started)
---
Enable Entire with session tracking for your AI agent workflows.

If Entire is not yet configured, this runs the full configuration flow.
If Entire is already configured but disabled, this re-enables it.

Existing git hooks are kept: each is moved to <hook>.pre-entire and runs after
Entire's hook.

If the current directory is not a git repository, Entire can initialize one
for you and create an initial commit. It never creates or pushes to a remote —
publish the repository yourself when you're ready.

Usage:
  entire enable [flags]

Flags:
      --absolute-git-hook-path[=true|false]   Embed full binary path in git hooks (for GUI git clients that don't source shell profiles)
      --agent string                          Agent to set up hooks for (e.g., antigravity, claude-code, codex, copilot-cli, cursor, factoryai-droid, opencode, pi; external agents on $PATH are also available). Enables non-interactive mode.
      --agent-help-skill[=true|false]         Install the stable Entire agent-help skill (points agents at entire agent-help) for selected agent(s)
      --checkpoint-backend string             Checkpoint storage backend: refs (default; one git ref per checkpoint) or branch (legacy shared entire/checkpoints/v1 branch)
      --checkpoint-push-remote string         Git remote for checkpoint uploads (saved to .entire/settings.local.json, even with --project)
      --checkpoint-remote string              Checkpoint remote in provider:owner/repo format; providers: github, gitlab (e.g., github:org/checkpoints-repo)
  -f, --force[=true|false]                    Force reinstall hooks (removes existing Entire hooks first)
  -h, --help[=true|false]                     help for enable
      --import-history[=true|false]           During first-time setup, import the selected agents' existing session history (last 30 days) without prompting
      --init-repo[=true|false]                If not a git repo, initialize one non-interactively
      --initial-commit-message string         Commit message for the initial commit when bootstrapping a new repo
      --local[=true|false]                    Write settings to .entire/settings.local.json instead of .entire/settings.json
      --no-init-repo[=true|false]             If not a git repo, exit instead of prompting to initialize one
      --project[=true|false]                  Write settings to .entire/settings.json even if it already exists
      --search-skill[=true|false]             Install the optional Entire search skill for selected agent(s)
      --skip-initial-commit[=true|false]      Don't create the initial commit when bootstrapping a new repo
      --skip-push-sessions[=true|false]       Disable automatic pushing of session logs on git push
      --telemetry[=true|false]                Enable anonymous usage analytics (default true)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]                      Accept all defaults without prompting (in a non-repo directory: init git and commit; then enable all agents and accept telemetry). In an existing repository it lists the configuration files to commit rather than committing them. Does not import existing agent history — see --import-history

Global Flags:
      --context name   Act as this saved login name for this command only — including the git and agent processes it spawns — instead of the active context (entire auth contexts lists them)
---
Manage where a repository is mirrored across Entire clusters

Usage:
  entire repo mirror [flags]
  entire repo mirror [command]

Available Commands:
  add         Mirror a repository onto one or more clusters
  detach      Convert a GitHub mirror into a native Entire repository
  list        List repos you can see: existing mirrors and GitHub repos you could onboard
  remove      Remove a repository's mirrors from one or more clusters
  resync      Queue a fresh sync of a GitHub mirror on every cluster

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for mirror

Global Flags:
      --context name   Act as this saved login name for this command only — including the git and agent processes it spawns — instead of the active context (entire auth contexts lists them)

Use "entire repo mirror [command] --help" for more information about a command.

They're less trivial than they look. Step 7 is the real work, and most of it needs you at Vultr.

**Step 6: not yours.** The hardware check is Person 3's job (Isaac): charge the Quest, test WebXR passthrough and hand tracking, and install COLMAP and MediaPipe on his Mac. One item is yours. The step also says to test an ElevenLabs Instant Voice Clone in the web app with a minute of speech, using the mic you'll use for the interview. That fits the voice work, but it needs you to talk into the mic.

**Step 7: the server (yours).** It has three parts.

| Part | What it is | Who can do it |
|---|---|---|
| A1–A3 | Copy your SSH key, add it in Vultr, create a 2 GB Ubuntu 24.04 instance (about $10–12/month from the credits, backups off) | You, in the Vultr dashboard. I can't use it. |
| A4–A8 | SSH in, open ports 80 and 443, install Caddy and Node 22, set up HTTPS with a placeholder page at `<ip-with-dashes>.sslip.io` | I can run these over SSH once you give me the IP |
| A9 | Open the address on the laptop and the Quest and confirm the padlock | You, on the Quest |
| A10 | Write the IP into `DEPLOY.md`, the `SERVER=` line in `deploy.sh`, and the deploy skill | Those are Ethan's shared files, so he approves it |
| B1–B5 | Log the server into GitHub, clone the repo, copy `.env` up, set up the systemd service | I can do the commands. You do the GitHub login in your browser. |
| C | The first real deploy | Ethan, at hour 3–4. There's no app yet. |

**Step 8: not a task for me.** It's the three of you together: read `DESIGN-RULES.md` and `PLAN.md`, fill in BUILD.md's timing section once Hack Western's schedule is out, agree sleep shifts, check your accounts and keys, and pack.

**Before I touch a server:**
- Creating the instance spends Vultr credits. Please do that yourself, or tell me clearly to go ahead once it exists.
- Part A4 onward runs commands as root on a remote machine. I'd tell you what I ran and why, as the setup doc suggests.
- B1 says the repo is private, but Ethan told you to skip the private-repo part of Step 5. Is the repo public? That decides whether the server needs `gh auth login` at all.

**What I need to start on A4–A8:**
1. The server's IP address, and the Vultr instance running.
2. Confirmation that your SSH key is on it (A1–A2).
3. An OK to run those commands over SSH.

Do you have a Vultr account with credits yet? If not, that's the first thing to do, and it's on the "Humans only" list in BUILD.md.

Step 9: at kickoff, run your agents the Ben Zhou way
  Claude credits are tight, so each person runs one agent for their own work (two at most),
  and the team adds a few special-job agents at set times. The goal for hour 4 is a saved
  head talking in the headset with a cloned, aged voice; everything else builds on that.


  Start your agent
     1. Person 1 fills in the last two blanks in CONTRACTS.md: the voice pipeline and the head
        files.
     2. Open your agent in one terminal tab and turn on /remote-control . Paste:

      You're my agent. I'm [Person 1, 2 or 3] and I own [folders]. Read CLAUDE.md and
      everything it loads. Work on one task at a time in my folders: plan it, show me the plan
      before writing code, build it, prove it works, commit, and post on the board when a
      teammate depends on it. Start with my next unchecked step in BUILD.md. Check the
      board with tools/board unread before each new task.


     3. For each task, give it a brief:

      Build: [the feature, in 2-3 sentences] in [folder]/. Read [folder]/README.md first.
      Follow the "[section]" part of CONTRACTS.md. Done means: [what should work], it
      runs without errors, and you've committed. Check it by: [running the tests / opening
      the page and taking a screenshot]. Then give me your summary (see CLAUDE.md).

  Open a second tab only when two tasks can really run at the same time, like the fine-tune
  or a head build running while you work on something else. Keep it to a different folder
  from your first agent (or a separate git worktree ), and close it when that task is done.




                                                                                            Page 13 of 18
 Uncle: Team Setup




  Saving credits
          /clear between unrelated tasks, so the agent isn't re-reading a long old
         conversation with every message.
         Sonnet for routine work; switch to Opus with /model only for hard problems, like the
         simulation math or the head pipeline.
         Plan mode (Shift+Tab) first: a wrong 20-minute build is the most expensive thing an
         agent can do.
         Don't leave tools/board wait running; every wake-up costs credits. Check
          tools/board unread between tasks instead.
         Have agents search with entire graph search instead of reading files blindly, and
         note the savings for the Entire prize page.


  Your routine, all weekend
         Check your agent every 10 to 15 minutes. Read its summary, answer questions, and
         give the next task.
         Stuck for 20 minutes? Press Esc, explain it differently, or split the task smaller.
         Ask for proof of every "done": a test result, a screenshot or a number.
         Every hour or so, ask your agent where your part is at in five sentences and what's
         risky.


  Special-job agents
  Ben ran agents with one job each at set points. Open each in its own tab when its time
  comes:

README.md
# Deploying Uncle

Only Person 1 deploys. The app lives on the live HTTPS link from the first hours, and everyone tests there, because the Quest's browser needs HTTPS for WebXR and the microphone.

## The server (filled in by Person 2 after setting it up)

- Provider: Vultr Cloud Compute, Toronto, Ubuntu 24.04
- IP address: 144.202.9.158
- Address: https://144-202-9-158.sslip.io (later: the GoDaddy Registry domain)
- Web server: Caddy, config at `/etc/caddy/Caddyfile`
- App service: `uncle` (systemd, `/etc/systemd/system/uncle.service`), runs `npm start` in `/root/uncle`
- App port: 3000
- Keys: `/root/uncle/.env` (copied up with `scp`, never committed)

## How the app must be set up

- `npm start` from the repo's main folder starts everything: the WebXR page and the API, on port 3000 (or `PORT` from `.env`).
- If the front end needs building, package.json has a `build` script; `deploy.sh` runs it.
- The app starts even when a key is missing, and says which feature is off.

## Deploying

1. Everyone has pushed what should go live.
2. Run the quick test (once it exists): it checks the main demo flow on the live link.

- **Stock voice first:** the clone needs the interview recording, which doesn't exist yet. The aging filter doesn't depend on whose voice it is.

content.text:
Task 2, the one-line voice loop, is built and committed locally as `06871ef`. I haven't pushed it. It runs on this laptop but isn't live yet.

**What changed**
- **`voice/filter.js`:** the aging filter. It changes pitch and pace separately (the pitch shifts without the speech speeding up). It adds a wobble in pitch and loudness, takes some brightness off the top, and adds a little breath noise that only appears while the voice is speaking.
- **`voice/aging.js`:** a "how aged" slider from 0 to 1, plus separate settings for male, female and unknown voices.
- **`voice/tts.js`:** the ElevenLabs call, using the stock voice "Will".
- **`voice/wav.js`:** turns the audio into a `.wav` file the browser can play.
- **`server/index.js`:** a new `/api/voice/test` route (`?raw=1` returns the original voice, and `?strength=` sets how aged it is).
- **`server/public/index.html`:** a test page with Play original, Play aged, a slider and a voice-type dropdown.
- **Tests:** 13 pass, and the suite passed 25 times out of 25. The new filter tests check pitch and speed on a synthetic tone with a known pitch.

**How to check**
- **Listen:** run `npm start`, open `localhost:3000`, and press the two buttons. The page shows the delay each time.
- **Audio files:** I saved both versions in the scratchpad folder. The originals are `original.wav` and `aged-neutral.wav` in `/private/tmp/claude-502/-Users-jeffreywongbusiness-hack-western-2026-uncle/fc3c57fe-3193-4417-99cf-ef495d02437c/scratchpad/`.
- **Measured here:** ElevenLabs first byte took 434 ms, and the whole line (about 4.5 s of speech) took 671 ms. The aging filter took 55–69 ms. The aged clip is 8.7% longer, which matches the intended pace of 0.92.

**What I'm unsure about**
- **I can't hear it.** The tests prove pitch and speed change as intended. They don't prove it sounds like a believable older person, so please listen and tell me what's off (too robotic, too breathy and so on). The sliders are there for tuning.
- **The aging amounts aren't researched yet.** They're my first guesses, marked "provisional" in the code. PLAN.md requires checking each against voice-aging research and citing it. I'll do that before we tune further.
- **The delay numbers aren't the real target.** They cover the text-to-speech and filter steps only. The 1.2 s goal is from the end of the user's speech to the first word, and that needs speech-to-text and the model, which don't exist yet.
- **Test slip:** my first attempt to fix a flaky test made it fail every time, so I fixed that too. The final version passed 25 runs.

Do you want me to push this and post on the board? After that, I'd research the aging numbers so the filter has real citations. Or you can listen first and tell me what to change.

content.text:
Good, that's the answer. The cause is how my breath effect works. It follows the loudness of the speech very closely, so every hard "t" or "k" gets a burst of hiss that cuts off quickly, which sounds like a snare. Real breathiness is a soft, steady bed of air under the voice, so I'll rebuild it that way:
- It follows a slow average of the loudness (tens of milliseconds) instead of every peak.
- It uses band-limited noise, so there is no harsh top end.
- It is quieter overall. The new noise sits about 24 dB below the voice, where before it was about 16 dB below and spiky.
